zh.title: 地球怎样走过45.4亿年？
zh.intro: 拖动时间，找一条岩石留下的线索。先看漫长的全程，再放大动物和人类出现的最近一小段。
zh.timelineTitle: 把很久很久，放在同一把尺上
zh.timelineHint: 拖动下面的时间滑块，也可以点击标尺或选择一条线索。时间由左边的古老，走向右边的今天。
zh.overviewNote: 这条总轴始终保持真实线性时间比例。竖线是定位记号，不表示事件持续长度；相近线索会重叠。
zh.zoomNote: 每个窗口内部都等比例。更换窗口会换一把尺，时间本身不会加速。
zh.zoomScale: 同样宽度，这个窗口比全程放大 {factor} 倍。
zh.interval: 约24亿—21亿年前的持续转变；彩带表示近似区间。
zh.allDates: 日期都是近似值。全程用地球年龄常用估计约45.4亿年；形成往往有过程，标记不是精确的诞生日。更古老的太阳系材料、最老地球矿物与地球年龄，也不能互相替代。
zh.compressed: 把全程想成1米：智人约30万年的片段只有约0.066毫米，屏幕上可能小于一个像素。标记加粗只是方便定位。
zh.historyNotLadder: 这不是通往人类的阶梯。细菌、藻类、植物和动物的不同支系一直共同改变地球；许多分支也已经灭绝。
zh.deepTimeTitle: 深入：这条线索怎样被读出来？
zh.dating: 岩层上下关系给出先后顺序，某些矿物的铀—铅等放射性时钟约束古老年代。碳—14主要适用于近几万年内的含碳材料，不能给45.4亿年的地球定年。侵蚀、变质和保存机会会让记录缺页；最早找到的证据说明“那时已经存在”，不等于起源时刻。
zh.oxygenTitle: 小实验：有产氧，为什么空气仍可能不积氧？
zh.oxygenIntro: 让同一份氧气账单走几回合：光合作用释放氧；有机物的有氧呼吸和分解会用掉一部分；含还原性物质的海水、岩石和气体还能继续耗氧。只有没有被抵消的部分才留存。
zh.oxygenBoundary: 这是教学收支模型，所有量用任意“氧气单位”，每回合没有对应年数。留存池不区分海洋和大气，不预测古大气氧浓度，也不直接生成动物或预测动物何时起源；记账顺序不是地球上反应发生的先后。
zh.recycleControl: 本轮有机物有氧回用比例
zh.recompute: 改变条件会用新条件重算当前回合数；拖回去，再前进，会得到相同结果。
zh.stockResultZero: 一直有氧气释放，但到这一回合，来源仍被消耗抵消，自由氧没有净留存。
zh.stockResultGrowth: 到这一回合，部分氧气超过了消耗量，于是能留存。耗氧反应仍在进行，并没有全部消失。
zh.stockResultStart: 第0回合还没有发生账目变化。保持条件，往前走一回合。
zh.chartTitle: 相同来源、相同有氧回用，比较两条留存曲线
zh.referenceStock: 固定需求2的对照，当前留存 {stock} 单位。
zh.chartDescription: 横轴是教学回合，纵轴是自由氧留存任意单位。实线显示当前设置，虚线只把地质耗氧需求改为每回合2单位。两条线使用同一标尺。
deepOxygen: 光合作用把二氧化碳和水变成有机物并释放氧。有机物再被有氧呼吸或分解，相应的氧就会被消耗。因此，长期积氧还与有机碳能否暂存、埋藏而不立刻重新氧化有关。这里用“本轮有氧回用比例”把这件事单独拿出来试。未回用的那部分有机碳留在本模型活跃分解池之外。
这个账本每回合先扣去有氧回用，再满足地质耗氧需求。实际地质消耗不能大于可用氧，剩余自由氧绝不会为负。现实中的呼吸、气体交换、风化、铁和硫反应同时发生，还受营养、气候与海洋混合影响；这里的扣款顺序只是教学记账。
地质耗氧需求每回合重新提供，不是一个最后必然被清空的全球水桶。实验中的两组对照说明“来源与消耗的平衡可以改变”，不能单独证明真实大氧化的某一种触发机制。古大气的变化还包含长期反馈和反复波动。
zh.rockTitle: 岩石也会记账：条带状含铁地层
zh.rockIntro: 海水中溶解的亚铁被氧化后，可以形成不易溶解的含铁颗粒并沉积。经过成岩和后来的变化，部分记录保存成富铁层与富硅层交替的岩石。
zh.rockDiagramLabel: 溶解铁的氧化与沉积路径示意，及交替岩层的示意剖面；不是实测厚度或每年的层数。
zh.ironRecord: 沉积 → 成岩 → 留下记录
zh.rockMore: 深入：看到红色条带，就知道当时空气富氧吗？
rockEvidence: 不能只凭颜色下结论。条带状含铁地层记录铁的迁移、氧化和沉积；其中一些铁的氧化可以有分子氧参与，也有不用释放氧的微生物光合作用途径。富铁层不是全球大气含氧量的单一刻度。
研究者把不同地点的岩层年代、铁和硫同位素、矿物与其他沉积记录放在一起比较。硫同位素信号的长期改变，是研究大气积氧的重要线索之一。大氧化也不是24亿年前一次按键，就把整个海洋与空气变成今天的样子。

formation.title: 小天体聚成地球
formation.lead: 地球不是突然冒出来的完整蓝色球。绕年轻太阳运动的尘埃与小天体一次次聚集、碰撞，逐渐长成行星。
formation.mechanism: 重力帮助物质聚集；碰撞、压缩和放射性衰变带来热。形成中的地球经历强烈加热，有的区域熔融，给内部物质重新分配创造了条件。
formation.evidence: 陨石、地球矿物与月球样品中的放射性时钟共同约束太阳系早期历史。地球的常用年龄估计约45.4亿年；全程标尺采用这一近似值。
formation.uncertainty: 不存在一块保存了全部形成过程的“生日石”。年龄估计也不表示地球在某一天完成了吸积、地核、海洋和大气。
formation.question: 如果长成一颗行星需要不断碰撞，为什么“刚诞生的地球”不可能立刻像今天？

separation.title: 内部开始分家：金属向下，岩石在外
separation.lead: 当地球的某些部分足够热、能够流动时，密度较大的金属向内部汇集，较轻的硅酸盐物质留在外层。
separation.mechanism: 这个过程叫分异。它把早期混合物重新分配为富金属的核心与岩石外层。冷却、熔融和地壳的生成后来仍在继续，不是一次分家就得到今天每一层。
separation.evidence: 地球的分层结构、陨石中的金属与岩石，以及行星材料的实验共同支撑分异的解释。图上的约45亿年，是早期过程的示意锚点。
separation.uncertainty: 不能把今天固态内核的形成日期，直接当成早期地核分离的日期。两者不是同一件事。
separation.question: 如果材料完全不能流动，只看谁比较重，足以让它们马上分层吗？

moon.title: 一次巨大碰撞怎样留下月球？
moon.lead: 主流假说认为：年轻地球与另一个大型天体发生巨大碰撞，进入轨道的物质参与形成了月球。
moon.mechanism: 月球样品保留了高温熔融的线索，地月岩石在一些同位素组成上也十分相似。研究者用碰撞模型检验哪些条件能留下合适的月球与地月系统。
moon.evidence: 阿波罗带回的样品改变了早期捕获说等解释的地位。约45亿年前是近似定位，碰撞时间、参与物质与后续形成过程仍在研究。
moon.uncertainty: 这幅时间标记不是拍到的一次碰撞；“某一种模型能做到”也不等于已经确定了所有真实碰撞细节。
moon.question: 一块月球岩石，可以怎样帮助我们判断几十亿年前发生过什么？

water.title: 小小锆石，留下早期水的线索
water.lead: 约44亿年前的一些锆石，比今天保存下来的绝大多数完整岩石还古老。它们内部的化学记录提示：很早就有物质与液态水相互作用。
water.mechanism: 锆石结晶时会保存一部分元素与同位素信息。研究者先给晶体定年，再结合氧同位素等特征，推断形成它的岩浆曾混入与地表液态水作用过的材料。
water.evidence: Jack Hills锆石研究提供了约44亿年前地壳与水环境的间接证据。晶体像幸存的小纸片，原来所在的大岩石可能早已被改造。
water.uncertainty: 水的线索不等于已画出当时全球海洋的地图，更不能据此宣称那时一定已有生命。
water.question: 为什么一粒晶体活下来了，却不能保证整块远古岩石也活下来？

life.title: 到约35亿年前，岩石里已有生命线索
life.lead: 早期舞台的主角很小：微生物。它们的活动、群落和留下的结构，有时能被岩石保存。
life.mechanism: 微生物席能捕捉沉积物，或影响矿物形成；一层层结构后来可能成为叠层石。研究者会把形状、环境和化学信号一起检查，排除非生命过程的解释。
life.evidence: 约35亿年前已有多类微生物活动记录。更老岩石和矿物中的一些候选证据仍有争论；新的发现还可能补上更早的一页。
life.uncertainty: “目前找到约35亿年前的证据”不是“生命恰好在35亿年前诞生”。也不能把所有早期叠层石都认作产氧蓝细菌制造。
life.question: 如果最早的一页丢失了，我们还能把第一张找到的纸当作这本书的开头吗？

oxygen.title: 大氧化：来源与消耗的平衡改变了
oxygen.lead: 有些微生物能利用阳光，从水中取得电子并释放氧。但释放出来的氧，还要面对海水、岩石、气体和生命活动的消耗。
oxygen.mechanism: 在长期收支有利于留存时，大气中的氧才显著积累。约24亿—23亿年前常概括关键转变，广义过程可延伸到约21亿年前，期间还有波动。它改变了许多微生物的生存条件。下面的实验可以亲手改变这本账。
oxygen.evidence: 不同地点的岩层年代、硫同位素与其他地球化学记录共同约束大氧化。蓝细菌的产氧起源早于显著大气积氧，但精确起点仍在研究。
oxygen.uncertainty: 没有“所有耗氧汇都耗尽”的全球开关。此后空气也没有立刻达到今天约21%的氧，深海和浅海的变化更不完全同步。
oxygen.question: 同样释放8份氧，如果别处每回合会用掉8份，还能在空气里越存越多吗？

eukaryotes.title: 细胞内部出现更复杂的分工
eukaryotes.lead: 在很长的微生物历史中，具有细胞核和内部结构的真核细胞也出现了。复杂不等于体积一定很大。
eukaryotes.mechanism: 真核生物的细胞里可以有细胞核与不同的细胞器。线粒体与叶绿体的历史和古老的细胞共生有关；这是细胞演化中的合作路径，并不是今天所有细菌都要走的下一步。
eukaryotes.evidence: 约19亿—14亿年前的地质记录已经提供真核生物的线索，约18亿年在这里作为近似路标。判断化石属于哪条支系，仍须结合多种特征。
eukaryotes.uncertainty: 这不是核细胞的精确诞生日；“真核”“多细胞”“动物”也不是三个可以互换的词。
eukaryotes.question: 一个真核生物可以只有一个细胞吗？一个多细胞生物一定是动物吗？

multicellular.title: 许多细胞，开始共同生活与分工
multicellular.lead: 多细胞生活在不同支系中多次出现。约10亿年前的红藻化石，就是一条值得放大的线索。
multicellular.mechanism: Bangiomorpha化石显示细胞有组织地排列，有些部分具有不同形态。多细胞的关键不只是挤在一起，还可能包括连接、协作和分工。
multicellular.evidence: 包含化石的岩层被相邻沉积岩的Re—Os定年约束在约10.47亿年前。这是保存较好、可用来研究早期真核演化的一条记录。
multicellular.uncertainty: 它不是所有多细胞生命的共同诞生日，也不是第一只动物。不同支系的多细胞化有不同历史。
multicellular.question: 一群各做各的细胞，与互相连接、分工的细胞群，有什么不同？

ediacaran.title: 海底出现叶片、条带与“被子”般的身体
ediacaran.lead: 到约5.8亿年前，一些海底群落留下了奇妙的大型软体生物印痕，形状与很多今天的动物不太一样。
ediacaran.mechanism: 身体可以平铺海底，也可以向水中伸展。软身体本来不容易留下化石，特殊沉积与保存条件让我们能看到这些古老生态系统的一角。
ediacaran.evidence: 埃迪卡拉生物群来自多个地区的沉积岩。印痕、活动痕迹与相关地层，让研究者重建它们的生活方式。
ediacaran.uncertainty: 不是每一个叶片形化石都是植物，也不是每一种都能稳妥归入今天某一动物类群。保存下来的群落也不代表当时所有生命。
ediacaran.question: 只看到身体留下的印痕，我们能知道哪些事，又还缺哪些事？

cambrian.title: 寒武纪：化石中的动物世界变丰富
cambrian.lead: 从约5.39亿年前开始的寒武纪，动物化石里的身体构造、硬壳与活动方式显著变丰富。
cambrian.mechanism: 捕食、钻洞、运动与防护改变了彼此的生存条件；硬的身体部分也更容易保存。环境变化、生态互动和发育创新都参与了这段历史。
cambrian.evidence: 研究者比较不同地点、不同层位的化石与活动痕迹。本馆用539百万年前的圆整入口；正式寒武纪底界为538.8 ± 0.6 Ma。伯吉斯页岩中约508 Ma的Waptia化石是更晚的一处生活记录，不能拿它当寒武纪开端。
cambrian.uncertainty: “大爆发”跨越数千万年，不是同一天出现所有动物；在它之前已经有动物与其他多细胞生物。化石变多也不全等于真实数量以同样比例增加。
cambrian.question: 如果硬壳比软身体更容易保存，化石本身会偏爱记录谁？

plants.title: 植物的微小孢子，留下登陆证据
plants.lead: 陆地不是突然长出大森林。约4.7亿年前的岩层中，微小孢子为早期陆生植物留下线索。
plants.mechanism: 走出水环境后，植物要面对失水、支撑和繁殖的新条件。早期记录里常见的是耐保存的微小孢子，完整植株要难找得多。
plants.evidence: 分散孢子与含孢子的植物碎片，把早期陆生植物的历史连接起来。孢子记录可以早于清楚保存的较大型植物化石。
plants.uncertainty: 这是陆生植物线索的近似时代，不能当作第一个生命踏上陆地的日期。微生物等的陆地活动有自己的、更早的历史。
plants.question: 为什么一粒孢子，可能比它来自的整棵植物更容易留在岩石里？

arthropods.title: 节肢动物也在陆地留下身体
arthropods.lead: 到约4.25亿年前，陆地节肢动物的化石已经留下记录。它们比四足脊椎动物更早成为陆地故事的一部分。
arthropods.mechanism: 离开水后，身体支撑、防止失水与呼吸都要应对新条件。不同动物支系用不同方式解决问题，登陆也可能有反复和不同程度。
arthropods.evidence: 苏格兰等地的古老节肢动物化石，与植物和沉积环境一起提供早期陆地生态的线索。这里选择约425百万年前作为一个记录锚点。
arthropods.uncertainty: 并非所有节肢动物同一时刻登陆，也不能用这一件化石给“第一只陆地动物”按下秒表。
arthropods.question: 水里能支持身体，到了空气中，支撑和呼吸会遇到哪些变化？

tetrapods.title: 有四肢，不代表已经能在岸上走
tetrapods.lead: 约3.65亿年前前后，早期四足脊椎动物处在水与陆地生活的多种尝试中。一些带趾的肢体仍在水中发挥作用。
tetrapods.mechanism: 肢体、脊柱、呼吸和感觉系统的变化并不同步。“长腿”到“能在陆地上承重行走”之间，还有许多结构与生活方式的差别。
tetrapods.evidence: 化石骨骼、关节形态和岩层环境帮助研究者判断动物如何活动。较晚的记录中，可以更清楚看到适于陆地行走的身体。
tetrapods.uncertainty: 这不是一条鱼突然爬上岸并变成所有陆地动物的时刻。它是一棵分支很多的演化树中的长期变化。
tetrapods.question: 一只动物有脚趾，为什么还不能单凭这一点断定它常在陆地走路？

permian.title: 二叠纪末：生态系统遭遇重大危机
permian.lead: 约2.52亿年前，更细写约251.9 Ma，海洋和陆地许多生物类群受到重创。这是地球记录中最严重的大灭绝之一。
permian.mechanism: 西伯利亚大火成岩省的大规模岩浆活动及相关气体释放，引发增温、海洋缺氧与酸化等环境压力；生物面对的是一串相互作用的后果。
permian.evidence: 化石在岩层中的消失、地球化学变化与火山岩年代，让研究者比较危机的节奏和环境条件。
permian.uncertainty: 全部生命没有消失。幸存支系随后重组生态系统，已灭绝物种不会“复活”。不同地区和生态功能的恢复节奏不同，不能用一条固定倒计时代表全球恢复。
permian.question: 当海水变暖、可用氧又减少时，依赖氧的海洋动物可能同时遇到哪两道难题？

cretaceous.title: 白垩纪末：撞击改变了生命舞台
cretaceous.lead: 约6600万年前，巨大小行星撞击及其环境后果引发大灭绝，非鸟类恐龙等许多类群消失。
cretaceous.mechanism: 冲击造成的物质进入大气，改变光照和气候，影响光合作用与食物网。灾害不只发生在撞击点附近。幸存支系后来又继续分化。
cretaceous.evidence: 希克苏鲁伯撞击坑、边界层的物质和全球化石变化，构成强而对应的撞击证据。德干火山活动提供了同期环境背景，但不能仅因时间相近，就给两种解释同等的因果权重。
cretaceous.uncertainty: “恐龙全没了”不准确：鸟类是一支延续到今天的恐龙。灭绝也不意味着地球从头变成没有生命。
cretaceous.question: 如果阳光减少，为什么原本没有被直接撞到的动物也会受到影响？

humans.title: 智人：总轴上极细的一小段
humans.lead: 我们这一物种——智人——已有约30万年的化石与演化历史。把它放回45.4亿年的尺上，几乎挤在今天的边缘。
humans.mechanism: 放大最近100万年的窗口，才能容易看清这段时间。那只是换了一把时间尺，没有把人类的历史变得和早期微生物一样长。
humans.evidence: 非洲的化石和遗传研究帮助重建智人的起源与扩散；化石最初出现的范围也会随着发现和分类研究更新。
humans.uncertainty: 智人的起源不是所有人属成员的起源，也不是所有早期人类的历史。人类出现更不是演化预先设定的终点。
humans.question: 把智人的约30万年，与约35亿年前已有微生物的证据相比，哪个片段更长？

today.title: 今天：还在继续写的这一页
today.lead: 岩石、大气、海洋与生命仍然互相作用。今天的小小观察，也可以成为理解地球的一条线索。
today.mechanism: 微生物、植物和动物共同参与物质循环，人类活动也影响环境。古老历史帮助我们理解变化需要条件、会留下记录，并且有不同时间尺度。
today.evidence: 我们可以观察今天的岩石、生态系统和气体交换，再谨慎地与古代记录比较。相似过程提供线索，但环境不一定完全相同。
today.uncertainty: 地球历史不是安排好的剧本。理解过去，不代表可以用这条简化时间线准确预言未来。
today.question: 下一次看见一块带条纹的岩石，你最想先问它什么？

huronian.title: 休伦冰期背景：氧与气候在同一段历史中
huronian.lead: 在约24亿—21亿年前的大氧化转变附近，地球也留下了多次古老冰川活动的证据。这里把约23亿年前选作路标。
huronian.mechanism: 氧的增加可以改变大气中的甲烷等气体，而甲烷具有温室效应。气候、火山、岩石风化和生命活动彼此影响；冰期之间也可能有非冰期。
huronian.evidence: 含冰川搬运碎屑的沉积、地层对比与放射性定年，让研究者检验冰川和积氧变化的相对时序。
huronian.uncertainty: 两个过程出现在相近时代，不等于只靠“氧变多”就能完整解释每次冰期。古老地层的对比和具体时间仍有不确定性。
huronian.question: 如果一个变化改变了温室气体，它可能怎样把微小生命的活动连接到全球气候？

cryogenian.title: 成冰纪：低纬度也留下冰川线索
cryogenian.lead: 约7.2亿—6.35亿年前的成冰纪，包含两次特别广泛的冰川活动，常被放在“雪球地球”的问题下研究。
cryogenian.mechanism: 冰雪反射阳光，会加强降温；火山释放、二氧化碳变化与岩石风化又能参与更长时间的反馈。冰扩张和退缩并不是同一个简单按钮。
cryogenian.evidence: 不同大陆保存的冰川沉积，与古地磁提供的古纬度信息一起，支撑低纬度冰川的解释。年代与冰后沉积也是重要线索。
cryogenian.uncertainty: “成冰纪”不代表整个约8500万年都被同样厚的冰盖封住。海冰是否完全覆盖、是否保留开水面与生命避难处，仍须比较模型和记录。
cryogenian.question: 为什么在古赤道附近找到冰川证据，会比只在古极地发现更让人惊讶？

ordovician.title: 奥陶纪末：冰、海平面与海洋生命危机
ordovician.lead: 约4.45亿—4.43亿年前，奥陶纪末的多阶段危机重创多种海洋生物，气候、冰川与海洋条件一起变化。
ordovician.mechanism: 降温与冰川增长、海平面下降会改变浅海栖息地；不同阶段的海水缺氧和后续环境转变又带来其他压力。不能只用一个温度箭头概括整场危机。
ordovician.evidence: 化石类群在地层中的变化、海平面与冰川沉积记录，可帮助研究者比较危机发生的先后。
ordovician.uncertainty: 大灭绝不能只按“掉了多少物种”排队。不同事件的环境条件、选择性与恢复过程并不一样。
ordovician.question: 如果许多动物住在浅海，海平面大幅下降会改变什么？

forests.title: 森林改变地表，也改变碳的去向
forests.lead: 约3.86亿年前，纽约州Cairo保存下来的古土壤和根系，记录了一种泥盆纪森林的地下结构。它是一个有地点、有年代的证据窗口。
forests.mechanism: 分枝根系改变植物与土壤的接触，影响风化、养分和水的流动。落下的有机物可能分解，也可能在合适环境中埋藏；更晚的石炭纪煤沼泽属于另一组环境与时间。
forests.evidence: Cairo的原地根系网络及其分布是直接证据。地上树干、叶片与树冠形态还需结合其他化石和比较重建，证据强度不能一概而论。
forests.uncertainty: 这里不宣称“最早森林”，也不把Cairo画成后来煤沼泽。森林不会必然变成煤；湿润环境、沉积空间、埋藏和保存等共同作用。古生代煤多不能简单归因于当时缺少降解木质素的真菌。
forests.question: 为什么同一棵倒下的树，可能很快分解，也可能有一部分碳被埋起来？

devonian.title: 晚泥盆世：一段反复的海洋危机
devonian.lead: 晚泥盆世在约3.72亿和3.59亿年前等时段发生多个生物危机脉冲，并非两者之间持续同样强度的一场灭绝。
devonian.mechanism: 部分脉冲保存了海洋缺氧证据。陆地植被、营养输入、气候和海洋循环可能相互影响；森林扩张不是所有地区、所有脉冲的唯一解释。
devonian.evidence: 化石消失的层位、黑色页岩等沉积和地球化学指标，让研究者检查哪些海域缺氧、变化何时发生。
devonian.uncertainty: 不能把整段时期说成一天发生的一次灾难，也不能把所有变化确定地归因于陆地植物。不同脉冲和地区可能有不同因素。
devonian.question: 如果河流把更多营养带入海洋，生物生长和分解为什么可能一起影响氧？

paleoIce.title: 晚古生代冰室：冰川会多次进退
paleoIce.lead: 约3.6亿—2.6亿年前的宽泛背景中，南方大陆多地有冰川记录；这里选择约3.2亿年前作为观察路标。
paleoIce.mechanism: 大陆位置、二氧化碳、植被和轨道变化在不同尺度上共同影响冰量。更细的地层显示冰川并非一直不变，而有多次进退和区域差异。
paleoIce.evidence: 冰川侵蚀、搬运沉积与浅海沉积中的海平面变化，帮助重建古冰量及其节奏。
paleoIce.uncertainty: 整条蓝带不是所有地方连续覆盖冰的长度，也不能把森林埋碳当作这段冰期唯一原因。
paleoIce.question: 同在一个漫长“冰期背景”里，两个相隔很久的地点一定会看到同样的冰吗？

triassic.title: 三叠纪末：另一次火山相关的灭绝
triassic.lead: 约2.01亿年前，更细的期界估计为201.4 ± 0.2 Ma，三叠纪末发生另一场大灭绝。它比白垩纪末撞击早得多。
triassic.mechanism: 中央大西洋大火成岩省（CAMP）的岩浆与气体释放与危机密切相关。熔体包裹体中的二氧化碳，为大量碳释放提供直接材料线索，其环境后果包括增温和海洋酸化。
triassic.evidence: 化石变化、岩浆岩年代与地球化学记录相互比较，帮助检验火山活动与危机的关系。
triassic.uncertainty: 并不是所有大灭绝都有一个撞击坑。也不能只因事件相邻就认定每条因果细节都已确定。
triassic.question: 比较这条线索与6600万年前的线索，你会寻找哪些相同或不同的证据？

antarctic.title: 约3400万年前：南极大冰盖显著增长
antarctic.lead: 地球并不是从诞生起就有今天的南极冰盖。约3400万年前的气候转变中，南极冰量出现显著扩张。
antarctic.mechanism: 长时期二氧化碳与海洋条件的变化，影响夏天的雪能否留下，进而影响冰盖增长。早期山地冰与后来的大冰盖不是同一个尺度。
antarctic.evidence: 海洋沉积中的氧同位素、冰川相关沉积和地貌，被用来重建降温与冰量；它们需要彼此校验。
antarctic.uncertainty: 这不是南极从此每个地方永远保持同样冰厚的日期，也不是南北半球冰盖同步诞生。
antarctic.question: 为什么要把山地冰川与覆盖大片大陆的冰盖分开讨论？

quaternary.title: 第四纪：多轮冰期，也有人类的历史
quaternary.lead: 第四纪从约258万年前延续到今天，包含多次冰量增长和退缩，也包含人类扩散与大型动物变化的历史。
quaternary.mechanism: 轨道改变阳光在季节和纬度之间的分配，冰反照率与温室气体等反馈会放大响应。不同地区并不同步地变成一幅冰地图。
quaternary.evidence: 冰芯、海洋沉积、冰川地貌与花粉等记录，可以互相对照冰量、温度与生态变化。
quaternary.uncertainty: 第四纪不是一整块持续覆盖所有大陆的冰。今天处在其中的全新世间冰期，而不是“地球上已经没有冰期”。
quaternary.question: 如果冬天很冷却夏天融得更多，冰盖一定会扩大吗？

lgm.title: 最近一次盛冰期：约2万年前的不同海岸线
lgm.lead: 约2.1万年前附近，大陆冰盖比今天广得多，海平面也低得多。这里是最近一次冰量高峰附近的近似路标。
lgm.mechanism: 更多水储存在陆地冰中，会使全球平均海平面降低。冰退后水回到海洋，海岸线与可通过的陆地连接也随之改变。
lgm.evidence: 冰川遗留地貌、沉积、珊瑚等海平面记录与定年，帮助重建最近一次盛冰期。USGS把这一高峰概括为约2万年前。
lgm.uncertainty: 不是整个地球冻结。冰量的最大值与某个地点最冷的时刻也不必严格相同。
lgm.question: 如果把海水暂时搬进大陆上的大冰盖，浅浅的大陆架会发生什么？

megafauna.title: 冰期末的大型动物：没有一个全球统一答案
megafauna.lead: 最近一次冰期结束前后，一些地区的大型动物消失，另一些支系幸存。猛犸等巨兽的故事与人类和环境变化相交。
megafauna.mechanism: 气候、植被和栖息地变化会改变食物与迁徙条件；人类影响也需按地区和物种检验。不同地方的消失并不是同一天。
megafauna.evidence: 骨骼、牙齿、环境沉积与可用的放射性定年，帮助比较动物变化、人类活动和气候的先后。这里约1.2万年前只是最近一段故事的路标。
megafauna.uncertainty: 不能把所有大型动物的灭绝都确定归因于同一种原因，也不能说所有猛犸在这个日期一起消失。
megafauna.question: 如果两个地区的巨兽在不同时间消失，你会怎样检验一个“全球同一天”的解释？

en.title: How did Earth change over 4.54 billion years?
en.intro: Drag through time and follow clues preserved in rocks. See the long story first, then enlarge the tiny recent chapters of animals and humans.
en.timelineTitle: Put deep time on one ruler
en.timelineHint: Drag the time slider, tap the ruler, or choose a clue. Older time is on the left; today is on the right.
en.overviewNote: This overview always uses a true linear time scale. Vertical marks locate clues; their widths do not show durations. Nearby clues can overlap.
en.zoomNote: Equal lengths mean equal durations within each window. Changing the window changes the ruler, not the speed of time.
en.zoomScale: At the same width, this window is enlarged {factor} times relative to the overview.
en.nearby: A nearby clue in Earth's story
en.interval: An extended transition about 2.4–2.1 billion years ago; the band shows an approximate interval.
en.allDates: Dates are approximate. The full span uses a common estimate of Earth's age, about 4.54 billion years. Formation takes time; a marker is not an exact birthday. Older Solar System materials, the oldest terrestrial minerals and Earth's age are distinct quantities.
en.compressed: On a one-metre ruler for the whole story, the roughly 300,000 years of Homo sapiens would occupy only about 0.066 mm, potentially less than one screen pixel. Wider marks only help you locate a clue.
en.historyNotLadder: This is not a ladder leading to humans. Different branches of bacteria, algae, plants and animals have continued to change Earth together; many branches have also gone extinct.
en.deepTimeTitle: Look closer: how do we read this clue?
en.dating: Rock-layer order gives relative ages; radioactive clocks such as uranium–lead in some minerals constrain ancient dates. Carbon-14 mainly applies to carbon-bearing material from the last few tens of thousands of years, not a 4.54-billion-year-old Earth. Erosion, metamorphism and preservation leave gaps. The earliest surviving evidence establishes 'already present then', not the exact time of origin.
en.oxygenTitle: Try it: why can oxygen production leave no buildup in the air?
en.oxygenIntro: Follow one oxygen ledger over several turns. Photosynthesis releases oxygen; aerobic respiration and decomposition use some of it. Reduced substances in seawater, rocks and gases can consume more. Only the uncancelled remainder is retained.
en.oxygenBoundary: This teaching budget uses arbitrary oxygen units, with no years per turn. Its retained pool does not separate ocean from atmosphere, predict ancient oxygen concentrations, generate animals or predict their origins. The ledger order is not a real sequence of Earth reactions.
en.recycleControl: Aerobic recycling of this turn's organic matter
en.recompute: Changing a condition recalculates all the inspected turns using that condition. Moving backward and forward gives the same result.
en.stockResultZero: Oxygen keeps being released, but consumption has cancelled the supply through this turn. There is no net retention of free oxygen.
en.stockResultGrowth: By this turn, some oxygen has exceeded consumption and can be retained. Oxygen-consuming reactions continue; they have not all disappeared.
en.stockResultStart: At turn 0, nothing has yet changed in the ledger. Keep the conditions and move forward one turn.
en.chartTitle: Same source and aerobic recycling; compare two retention curves
en.referenceStock: The fixed-demand-2 comparison has retained {stock} units so far.
en.chartDescription: The horizontal axis shows teaching turns; the vertical axis shows arbitrary units of retained free oxygen. The solid line uses your settings. The dashed line changes only geological demand to 2 units per turn. Both use the same scale.
en.deepOxygenTitle: Look closer: what is in this ledger?
deepOxygen: Photosynthesis converts carbon dioxide and water into organic matter and releases oxygen. Aerobic respiration or decomposition of that organic matter consumes corresponding oxygen. Long-term oxygen buildup therefore also depends on organic carbon being stored or buried without immediately being reoxidized. The recycling control isolates that idea. Unrecycled organic carbon is held outside this model's active decomposition pool.

The ledger deducts aerobic recycling first, then meets geological oxygen demand. Actual geological use cannot exceed available oxygen, and retained free oxygen cannot be negative. Real respiration, gas exchange, weathering and iron and sulfur reactions overlap and depend on nutrients, climate and ocean mixing. This deduction order is only a bookkeeping device.

Geological demand is supplied again every turn. It is not a finite worldwide bucket destined to empty. The two cases demonstrate that the balance between sources and consumption can change. They do not establish one particular trigger of the real Great Oxidation Event, which also involved long-term feedbacks and repeated fluctuations.
en.rockTitle: Rocks keep records too: banded iron formations
en.rockIntro: Oxidation of dissolved ferrous iron in seawater can form less-soluble iron-bearing particles that settle. After lithification and later alteration, some records survive as alternating iron-rich and silica-rich layers.
en.rockDiagramLabel: Schematic oxidation and deposition pathway for dissolved iron, with alternating rock layers. Thicknesses and layers per year are not measured.
en.rockMore: Look closer: do red bands prove an oxygen-rich atmosphere?
rockEvidence: Colour alone is not enough. Banded iron formations record iron transport, oxidation and deposition. Molecular oxygen can participate in some iron oxidation, but microbial photosynthetic pathways that do not release oxygen can also oxidize iron. An iron-rich band is not a single global atmospheric oxygen gauge.

Researchers compare rock ages, iron and sulfur isotopes, minerals and other sedimentary records from different places. Persistent changes in sulfur isotope signals are among the important clues to atmospheric oxygenation. The Great Oxidation Event was not one button press 2.4 billion years ago that made the entire ocean and atmosphere resemble today's.

formation.title: Small bodies build a planet
formation.lead: Earth did not appear as a finished blue ball. Dust and small bodies orbiting the young Sun gathered, collided and gradually built a planet.
formation.mechanism: Gravity helped material gather. Impacts, compression and radioactive decay supplied heat. Parts of the growing Earth melted, allowing its internal materials to redistribute.
formation.evidence: Radioactive clocks in meteorites, terrestrial minerals and lunar samples constrain early Solar System history. A common estimate for Earth's age is about 4.54 billion years; the full ruler uses that approximate value.
formation.uncertainty: No single 'birthday rock' preserves the entire formation process. The age does not mean that accretion, the core, oceans and atmosphere were all completed on one day.
formation.question: If building a planet takes repeated collisions, why would young Earth look different from today's?

separation.title: Metal moves inward; rock stays outside
separation.lead: When parts of Earth became hot and mobile enough, denser metal gathered toward the interior while lighter silicate material remained farther out.
separation.mechanism: This is differentiation. It redistributed an early mixture into a metal-rich core and rocky outer regions. Cooling, melting and crust formation continued afterward; the first separation did not instantly produce every modern layer.
separation.evidence: Earth's layered structure, metal and rock in meteorites, and experiments on planetary materials support this explanation. The roughly 4.5-billion-year marker only locates the early process schematically.
separation.uncertainty: The date when the modern solid inner core began growing is not the date of early core segregation. These are different events.
separation.question: If the materials cannot move at all, does density alone make them separate immediately?

moon.title: How could a giant impact leave a Moon?
moon.lead: The leading hypothesis is that a large body struck the young Earth, and material put into orbit contributed to the Moon's formation.
moon.mechanism: Lunar samples preserve evidence of intense melting. Some isotope compositions in Earth and Moon rocks are very similar. Researchers test which impact conditions can leave a suitable Moon and Earth–Moon system.
moon.evidence: Apollo samples changed the standing of earlier ideas such as capture. About 4.5 billion years ago is an approximate location; impact timing, material contributions and subsequent assembly remain under study.
moon.uncertainty: This marker is not a photographed collision. A model's ability to produce an outcome does not establish every detail of the actual impact.
moon.question: How can one Moon rock help us test an event billions of years ago?

water.title: Tiny zircons preserve clues to early water
water.lead: Some approximately 4.4-billion-year-old zircons are older than nearly all surviving intact rocks. Their chemistry suggests that material interacted with liquid water very early.
water.mechanism: A zircon preserves some chemical and isotope information as it crystallizes. Researchers date the crystal and combine oxygen isotopes with other features to infer that its source magma included material altered by surface liquid water.
water.evidence: Jack Hills zircon studies provide indirect evidence for crust and a watery environment about 4.4 billion years ago. A crystal can survive like a scrap of paper after its original rock has been transformed.
water.uncertainty: A clue to water does not map the whole ancient ocean, and it does not establish that life already existed.
water.question: Why can an ancient crystal survive even when its original rock does not?

life.title: By about 3.5 billion years ago, life left clues
life.lead: Early protagonists were tiny microbes. Their activities, communities and structures sometimes became preserved in rocks.
life.mechanism: Microbial mats can trap sediment or influence mineral formation. Layered structures may become stromatolites. Researchers check shape, setting and chemistry together to test alternatives that do not require life.
life.evidence: Several kinds of microbial activity are recorded by about 3.5 billion years ago. Some candidate evidence in older rocks and minerals remains debated, and discoveries may fill in an earlier page.
life.uncertainty: Evidence dating to roughly 3.5 billion years does not mean life began exactly then. Nor can every early stromatolite be assigned to oxygen-producing cyanobacteria.
life.question: If the first page is missing, can the first surviving page be called the beginning of the book?

oxygen.title: Great Oxidation: the balance changes
oxygen.lead: Some microbes use sunlight to obtain electrons from water and release oxygen. That oxygen still faces consumption by seawater, rocks, gases and living processes.
oxygen.mechanism: Atmospheric oxygen builds up significantly when the long-term balance allows retention. About 2.4–2.3 billion years ago summarizes a key transition; the broader process can extend to about 2.1 billion years ago, with fluctuations. It changed conditions for microbes. Try changing the ledger below.
oxygen.evidence: Rock ages, sulfur isotopes and other geochemical records from different places constrain the transition. Cyanobacterial oxygen production predates major atmospheric buildup, but its exact origin remains under study.
oxygen.uncertainty: There was no global switch when every oxygen sink ran out. Air did not immediately reach today's roughly 21% oxygen, and shallow and deep oceans did not change in lockstep.
oxygen.question: If eight units of oxygen are released and eight are consumed each turn, can oxygen keep piling up in the air?

eukaryotes.title: Cells develop more internal organization
eukaryotes.lead: During the long microbial story, eukaryotic cells with nuclei and internal structures appeared too. More internal complexity does not necessarily mean a large organism.
eukaryotes.mechanism: Eukaryotic cells can contain a nucleus and different organelles. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have histories rooted in ancient cell partnerships. This was a route through evolution, not a compulsory next step for every bacterium.
eukaryotes.evidence: Geological records by about 1.9–1.4 billion years ago provide eukaryotic clues. This ruler uses 1.8 billion as an approximate signpost. Assigning fossils to lineages still requires several features.
eukaryotes.uncertainty: This is not an exact birthday for nucleated cells. 'Eukaryote', 'multicellular' and 'animal' are not interchangeable words.
eukaryotes.question: Can a eukaryote consist of one cell? Must a multicellular organism be an animal?

multicellular.title: Many cells live and work together
multicellular.lead: Multicellular living arose in different lineages more than once. Red algal fossils from about a billion years ago are one clue worth enlarging.
multicellular.mechanism: Bangiomorpha fossils show organized cell arrangements, with different shapes in some parts. Multicellularity can involve connections, cooperation and division of labour, beyond merely crowding together.
multicellular.evidence: Re–Os dating of sedimentary rocks bracketing the fossil-bearing layer constrains its age to about 1.047 billion years. It is a useful preserved record for studying early eukaryotic evolution.
multicellular.uncertainty: It is not the shared birthday of all multicellular life and not the first animal. Different lineages have different histories of multicellularity.
multicellular.question: How does a crowd of independent cells differ from cells connected into a cooperative body?

ediacaran.title: Fronds, ribbons and quilt-like bodies on the seabed
ediacaran.lead: By about 580 million years ago, some seabed communities left impressions of remarkable large soft-bodied organisms, unlike many familiar animals.
ediacaran.mechanism: Bodies could lie across the seabed or extend into the water. Soft bodies are difficult to fossilize; unusual sediment and preservation conditions let us glimpse these ancient ecosystems.
ediacaran.evidence: Ediacaran organisms occur in sedimentary rocks from several regions. Impressions, activity traces and their rock layers help reconstruct ways of life.
ediacaran.uncertainty: A frond-shaped fossil is not necessarily a plant. Many cannot be confidently placed within a living animal group, and preserved communities do not represent all life at the time.
ediacaran.question: What can a body impression tell us, and what information might still be missing?

cambrian.title: Cambrian fossils reveal a richer animal world
cambrian.lead: In the Cambrian, beginning around 539 million years ago, animal structures, hard parts and ways of moving become much more diverse in the fossil record.
cambrian.mechanism: Predation, burrowing, movement and defence changed living conditions for other organisms. Hard parts also preserve more readily. Environmental change, ecological interactions and developmental innovations all contributed.
cambrian.evidence: Researchers compare fossils and activity traces across places and layers. The rounded entry is 539 million years; the formal Cambrian base is 538.8 ± 0.6 Ma. A roughly 508 Ma Waptia fossil from the Burgess Shale records a later living community, not the beginning of the Cambrian.
cambrian.uncertainty: The 'explosion' spanned tens of millions of years. All animals did not appear on one day; animals and other multicellular organisms existed earlier. More fossils do not translate directly into the same increase in living abundance.
cambrian.question: If shells fossilize more easily than soft bodies, which organisms might the fossil record favour?

plants.title: Tiny spores record plants on land
plants.lead: Large forests did not arrive at once. Tiny spores in rocks about 470 million years old provide clues to early land plants.
plants.mechanism: Outside water, plants faced new problems of drying, support and reproduction. Early records often contain durable tiny spores; whole plants are much harder to find.
plants.evidence: Dispersed spores and spore-bearing plant fragments connect parts of the early land-plant story. Spore records can predate clearly preserved larger plant fossils.
plants.uncertainty: This approximate era of land-plant evidence is not the date when the first life reached land. Microbial activity on land has its own earlier history.
plants.question: Why might a tiny spore survive in a rock more readily than the whole plant that made it?

arthropods.title: Arthropods leave bodies on land too
arthropods.lead: By about 425 million years ago, fossils record land arthropods. They were part of the terrestrial story before four-limbed vertebrates.
arthropods.mechanism: Leaving water changes the demands of support, water retention and breathing. Different animal lineages solved these problems differently, with repeated transitions and different degrees of land use.
arthropods.evidence: Ancient arthropod fossils in Scotland and elsewhere, alongside plants and their sedimentary settings, provide clues to early land ecosystems. This is a record anchored at approximately 425 million years ago.
arthropods.uncertainty: All arthropods did not move onto land at once, and one fossil cannot start an exact stopwatch for the 'first land animal'.
arthropods.question: When water no longer supports a body, what changes for its support and breathing?

tetrapods.title: Four limbs do not guarantee walking on land
tetrapods.lead: Around 365 million years ago, early four-limbed vertebrates had varied relationships with water and land. Some limbs with digits still worked in water.
tetrapods.mechanism: Limbs, backbone, breathing and sensory systems did not change all at once. There are many structural and lifestyle differences between having limbs and supporting a body while walking on land.
tetrapods.evidence: Fossil bones, joints and sedimentary environments help researchers infer movement. Later records show more clearly the bodies suited to terrestrial walking.
tetrapods.uncertainty: This was not one fish climbing ashore and becoming every land animal. It was prolonged change within a branching evolutionary tree.
tetrapods.question: Why do toes alone not prove that an animal regularly walked on land?

permian.title: End-Permian: a great ecological crisis
permian.lead: About 252 million years ago, more closely around 251.9 Ma, many marine and terrestrial groups suffered severe losses in one of Earth’s greatest recorded mass extinctions.
permian.mechanism: Siberian Traps large-scale magmatism and associated gas release drove interacting environmental stresses, including warming, ocean oxygen loss and acidification.
permian.evidence: Disappearances in the fossil record, geochemical changes and volcanic rock ages allow researchers to compare the crisis with environmental conditions.
permian.uncertainty: All life did not vanish. Surviving lineages reorganized ecosystems; extinct species did not return to life. Regions and ecological functions recovered at different rates, so one fixed countdown cannot represent global recovery.
permian.question: What two linked difficulties can warmer, less oxygenated seawater create for oxygen-dependent animals?

cretaceous.title: End-Cretaceous: an impact changes the stage
cretaceous.lead: About 66 million years ago, a large asteroid impact and its environmental consequences triggered a mass extinction, eliminating non-avian dinosaurs and many other groups.
cretaceous.mechanism: Material injected into the atmosphere changed light and climate, affecting photosynthesis and food webs. Consequences extended far beyond the impact site. Surviving branches continued to diversify.
cretaceous.evidence: The Chicxulub crater, boundary-layer materials and global fossil changes provide strong corresponding impact evidence. Deccan volcanism supplies an environmental backdrop; temporal proximity alone does not give the two explanations equal causal weight.
cretaceous.uncertainty: 'All dinosaurs vanished' is inaccurate: birds are a surviving dinosaur branch. Extinction did not return Earth to a lifeless beginning.
cretaceous.question: If sunlight decreases, why can animals far from the impact also be affected?

humans.title: Homo sapiens: a tiny sliver on the full ruler
humans.lead: Our species, Homo sapiens, has a fossil and evolutionary history of roughly 300,000 years. On the 4.54-billion-year ruler it nearly merges with today's edge.
humans.mechanism: Enlarging the last million years makes this interval easier to see. It only changes the ruler; human history does not become as long as the early microbial story.
humans.evidence: African fossils and genetic research help reconstruct our species' origin and dispersal. Discoveries and classification research can update the earliest known fossil range.
humans.uncertainty: The origin of Homo sapiens is not the origin of the whole genus Homo or the entire history of earlier humans. Humans were not evolution's predetermined destination.
humans.question: Which is longer: roughly 300,000 years of our species, or the time since evidence of microbes around 3.5 billion years ago?

today.title: Today: the page is still being written
today.lead: Rocks, air, oceans and life continue to interact. A small observation today can become a clue to understanding Earth.
today.mechanism: Microbes, plants and animals take part in material cycles, and human activities affect environments too. Deep history shows that change requires conditions, leaves records and operates on different time scales.
today.evidence: We can observe modern rocks, ecosystems and gas exchange, then compare them cautiously with ancient records. Similar processes offer clues without requiring identical environments.
today.uncertainty: Earth's story is not a prearranged script. Understanding its past does not make this simplified timeline an accurate prediction of its future.
today.question: The next time you see a banded rock, what would you like to ask it first?

huronian.title: Huronian ice-age context: oxygen and climate share a chapter
huronian.lead: Near the Great Oxidation transition about 2.4–2.1 billion years ago, Earth also preserves evidence of repeated ancient glaciation. The signpost here is about 2.3 billion years ago.
huronian.mechanism: Increasing oxygen can change atmospheric gases such as methane, a greenhouse gas. Climate, volcanoes, weathering and life interact; nonglacial intervals can separate glaciations.
huronian.evidence: Deposits containing glacially transported debris, correlations between layers and radioactive dates help test the relative timing of glaciation and oxygenation.
huronian.uncertainty: Similar timing does not mean rising oxygen alone explains every glaciation. Ancient correlations and exact timing remain uncertain.
huronian.question: How could a change in greenhouse gases connect microscopic life to global climate?

cryogenian.title: Cryogenian: glacial clues at low latitudes
cryogenian.lead: The Cryogenian, about 720–635 million years ago, includes two exceptionally widespread glaciations often studied under the Snowball Earth question.
cryogenian.mechanism: Reflective ice and snow can amplify cooling. Volcanic release, changing carbon dioxide and weathering contribute longer-term feedbacks. Ice advance and retreat are not one simple switch.
cryogenian.evidence: Glacial deposits on different continents, combined with ancient latitudes inferred from paleomagnetism, support low-latitude glaciation. Dates and postglacial deposits add constraints.
cryogenian.uncertainty: The period was not covered by an identical ice sheet for all 85 million years. Complete sea-ice cover, open-water refuges and survival conditions require comparisons of models with records.
cryogenian.question: Why is evidence of glaciers near the ancient equator more surprising than evidence near ancient poles?

ordovician.title: End-Ordovician: ice, sea level and a marine crisis
ordovician.lead: Around 445–443 million years ago, multiple end-Ordovician crisis phases severely affected marine groups amid changing climate, glaciers and oceans.
ordovician.mechanism: Cooling, growing glaciers and falling sea level changed shallow-sea habitats. Oxygen-poor water and subsequent environmental shifts imposed other pressures in different phases. One temperature arrow cannot explain the whole crisis.
ordovician.evidence: Fossil changes through rock layers, sea-level records and glacial deposits help researchers compare the sequence of events.
ordovician.uncertainty: Mass extinctions differ in their conditions, selectivity and recovery; they are more than a ranking of lost species.
ordovician.question: What changes for shallow-sea animals when sea level falls substantially?

forests.title: Forests change landscapes and carbon pathways
forests.lead: About 386 million years ago, ancient soils and roots preserved at Cairo, New York, recorded the underground structure of a Devonian forest: a window into one place and time.
forests.mechanism: Branching roots changed plant–soil contact, weathering, nutrients and water movement. Organic litter could decay or become buried in suitable conditions. Later Carboniferous coal swamps belong to a different environmental and temporal setting.
forests.evidence: Cairo’s in-place root networks and their distribution are direct evidence. Trunks, foliage and canopy form require other fossils and comparative reconstruction; these do not all have equal evidential support.
forests.uncertainty: This is not labelled the oldest forest or reconstructed as a later coal swamp. Forests do not inevitably become coal: wet settings, depositional space, burial and preservation matter. The Paleozoic coal peak cannot simply be assigned to the absence of lignin-degrading fungi.
forests.question: Why might one fallen tree decompose quickly while some carbon from another is buried?

devonian.title: Late Devonian: repeated marine crises
devonian.lead: The Late Devonian included crisis pulses around 372 and 359 million years ago, rather than one extinction operating at uniform strength throughout the intervening interval.
devonian.mechanism: Some pulses preserve evidence for ocean oxygen loss. Vegetation, nutrient inputs, climate and circulation may interact; forest expansion alone does not explain every pulse and region.
devonian.evidence: Fossil disappearances, deposits such as black shales and geochemical indicators help test where oxygen-poor water occurred and when changes happened.
devonian.uncertainty: This was not one disaster on one day, and every change cannot be confidently assigned to land plants. Different pulses and regions can involve different factors.
devonian.question: If rivers deliver more nutrients, how can both biological growth and decay affect ocean oxygen?

paleoIce.title: Late Paleozoic icehouse: repeated advances and retreats
paleoIce.lead: Within the broad context of about 360–260 million years ago, many southern continental regions preserve glacial records. The inspection signpost is about 320 million years ago.
paleoIce.mechanism: Continental positions, carbon dioxide, vegetation and orbital variations affect ice at different scales. Detailed strata show repeated advances, retreats and regional differences.
paleoIce.evidence: Glacial erosion and transported deposits, together with sea-level changes in shallow-marine strata, help reconstruct ice volume and its rhythms.
paleoIce.uncertainty: The whole blue band does not mean unbroken ice everywhere. Forest carbon burial was not the only cause of this icehouse.
paleoIce.question: Must two distant places within one long ice-age context have experienced identical ice cover?

triassic.title: End-Triassic: another volcanism-linked extinction
triassic.lead: About 201 million years ago, with a more detailed boundary estimate of 201.4 ± 0.2 Ma, another mass extinction closed the Triassic, long before the end-Cretaceous impact.
triassic.mechanism: Magmatism and gas release in the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) are closely linked to the crisis. Carbon dioxide in melt inclusions supplies direct material evidence for substantial carbon release; environmental consequences include warming and ocean acidification.
triassic.evidence: Fossil changes, dates of igneous rocks and geochemical records help test links between volcanism and the crisis.
triassic.uncertainty: Not every mass extinction comes with an impact crater. Similar timing does not settle every causal detail.
triassic.question: Compared with the 66-million-year clue, which kinds of evidence would you seek in common, and which might differ?

antarctic.title: About 34 million years ago: major Antarctic ice growth
antarctic.lead: Antarctica has not carried its modern ice sheet since Earth formed. A climate transition around 34 million years ago brought substantial Antarctic ice expansion.
antarctic.mechanism: Long-term carbon dioxide and ocean changes affect whether summer snow survives and ice sheets grow. Earlier mountain ice and later large ice sheets are different scales.
antarctic.evidence: Marine oxygen isotopes, glacially related deposits and landforms help reconstruct cooling and ice volume, with cross-checks among them.
antarctic.uncertainty: This did not fix every Antarctic location at one ice thickness forever. Northern and southern ice sheets did not originate simultaneously.
antarctic.question: Why distinguish a mountain glacier from an ice sheet covering a large continental area?

quaternary.title: Quaternary: many glacial cycles and a human story
quaternary.lead: The Quaternary extends from about 2.58 million years ago to today, including repeated ice growth and retreat, human dispersal and changes among large animals.
quaternary.mechanism: Orbital variations redistribute sunlight by season and latitude. Ice reflectivity and greenhouse gas feedbacks amplify responses; regions do not all change into one simultaneous ice map.
quaternary.evidence: Ice cores, marine sediments, glacial landforms and pollen records allow comparisons of ice volume, temperature and ecological change.
quaternary.uncertainty: The Quaternary is not one continuous ice cover across all continents. Today is its Holocene interglacial, not an Earth on which ice-age conditions have ceased to exist.
quaternary.question: If winters are cold but summers melt even more snow, must an ice sheet grow?

lgm.title: Last Glacial Maximum: different coastlines around 20,000 years ago
lgm.lead: Around 21,000 years ago, continental ice sheets were much larger and sea level was much lower. This is an approximate signpost near the last peak in ice volume.
lgm.mechanism: Storing more water in land ice lowers global mean sea level. As ice retreats, water returns to the ocean, shifting coastlines and land connections.
lgm.evidence: Glacial landforms and deposits, sea-level records such as corals, and dating help reconstruct the Last Glacial Maximum. USGS summarizes its timing as about 20,000 years ago.
lgm.uncertainty: The entire planet was not frozen. Maximum ice volume need not coincide exactly with the coldest moment at each location.
lgm.question: If seawater is stored in huge land ice sheets, what happens to shallow continental shelves?

megafauna.title: Large animals near the ice-age end: no single global answer
megafauna.lead: Near the end of the last glacial period, large animals disappeared in some regions while other lineages survived. Mammoths and other giants link human and environmental histories.
megafauna.mechanism: Climate, vegetation and habitat changes alter food and movement opportunities. Human impacts require regional and species-level tests. Disappearances did not occur on one day worldwide.
megafauna.evidence: Bones, teeth, environmental sediments and suitable radioactive dates help compare animal changes, human activity and climate. About 12,000 years ago is only a signpost for this recent chapter.
megafauna.uncertainty: One cause cannot be confidently assigned to every large-animal extinction. Nor did all mammoths vanish at this date.
megafauna.question: If giants disappeared at different times in two regions, how would you test an explanation requiring one worldwide day?
